title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The primary estimand was the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (single initial LLM generation per task reused across arms), with guarded episodes allowed up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Execution completed per plan (planned episodes = 480, completed = 480, model calls used = 240). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract, the guarded arm can change outcomes only if the shared candidate fails validation or a validator‑triggered repair is applied; in this run every shared candidate passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded quantitative outcomes, an artifact‑based mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast, and concrete recommendations to make future GVR evaluations informative for verifier causal effect.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation from high‑level operator intent to device configurations is central to NetOps. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic orchestration offer promise but text‑level correctness metrics do not capture ordering, dependency, and invariants required for safe application. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed against device images or simulators and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failures (ordering mistakes, transient invariant violations, protected‑resource touches) that text tests miss [1].

A recurring mitigation is the generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern: an LLM produces a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations appear [2,3]. Prior work demonstrates GVR‑style benefits for many syntactic and some semantic faults, but open questions remain about verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompt conditions and about experimental choices that enable informative paired contrasts between guarded and unguarded pipelines [2,4].

We preregistered a paired experiment to answer one narrowly scoped estimand: does adding a deterministic verifier (with a single permitted repair) reduce unsafe configuration applications relative to LLM‑only generation under shared_initial_candidate semantics? The study preserved preregistration, execution traces, and analysis artifacts; here we summarize the design, report the artifact‑grounded quantitative outcome, diagnose the null paired contrast, and give concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations for future experimental designs.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents have recently been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults rather than only textual fidelity; NetConfArena is a recent example [1]. Research on configuration and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators can enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design and fault type [2,4]. Surveys and position pieces synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising safety patterns for NetOps automation [3,5]. The evolution of configuration analysis tooling (e.g., Batfish) provides engineering precedent for verifier design and incremental verification [6].

Our contribution differs in combining (a) a preregistered paired estimand, (b) shared_initial_candidate semantics explicitly registered before execution, (c) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and (d) archival of per‑call and validator traces that permit mechanistic reconciliation of the measured estimand to execution artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and defined the primary estimand as the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate; unsafe_apply=1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied). The analysis executor used a paired contingency approach with bootstrap percentile CIs and an exact McNemar test (bootstrap resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729).

Design and generation semantics: The design was paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused by both arms. Under that contract, the guarded arm could only create a discordant outcome if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation or if the guarded pipeline applied a validator‑triggered repair (preregistered maximum = 1 repair per task). We selected N = 240 paired tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks). Adversarial prompts were generated under a fixed, blinded adversary protocol specified in the preregistration.

Adapter, model, and verifier: Execution used the declared hosted model gpt‑5‑mini and the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The deterministic verifier used in the guarded arm was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The adapter contract and verifier behavior were preregistered; runtime adherence to the shared_initial_candidate contract and provider call counts were audited as part of execution accounting.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: A deterministic emulator and validator produced binary final outcomes (safe vs unsafe) by applying generated configurations to synthetic device images and checking semantic invariants. Predeclared exclusions included items flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator reports unsafe) and infra failures after allowed retries; the retry policy allowed up to two infra recovery attempts. All missingness and exclusion rules were applied as preregistered and recorded in the execution archive.

Statistical analysis: The registered analysis executor estimated the paired difference from the paired contingency table (n11, n10, n01, n00), produced bootstrap percentile 95% CIs, and reported an exact two‑sided McNemar p‑value on discordant pairs. Secondary analyses (repair counts, model‑call budgets, subgroup slices) were specified but conditional on nondegenerate discordant pairs.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed per plan: planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete pairs = 240. Provider call accounting matched shared_initial_candidate semantics: model calls used = 240 (one initial generation per task). No infrastructure failures, no preregistered exclusions, and no 'possible false‑safe' flags occurred.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Condition aggregates show baseline successes = 240/240 and guarded successes = 240/240. The paired contingency is n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired estimate (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0. These numeric results are consistent across the preregistered subgroup partitions (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial), all of which are degenerate (zero unsafe applies in both arms).

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied; repair invocation count = 0 for all guarded episodes. Representative validator traces in the archive show detailed validation_before/validation_after snapshots and recorded difficulty labels, and they indicate deterministic PASS semantics for every shared candidate. Because the shared initial generation matched the guarded final configuration on all tasks and passed validation, the guarded arm could not produce discordant outcomes relative to baseline under the adapter contract.

Planned but unused sensitivity channels: The preregistration specified sensitivity analyses treating flagged 'possible false‑safe' items and infra failures as unsafe in worst‑case analyses; none of these cases occurred and the corresponding sensitivity channels were therefore not informative in this run.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics ensured exactly one LLM candidate per task was produced and reused across arms. The guarded arm is only a causal intervention to the extent the verifier (a) rejects the shared candidate or (b) triggers a repair that alters the final configuration. In this execution every shared candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs were invoked; as a result the guarded and baseline final configurations were identical for every task and the paired contingency is degenerate. This mechanistic account is directly traceable to the archived execution accounting and validator traces.

Design implications and experimental recommendations: To obtain an informative paired contrast for verifier causal effect, at least one of the following is required: (1) allow independent initial generations per arm so generator variability can create discordant candidates; (2) increase adversary strength or diversify adversarial strategies so initial candidates fail validation more often; or (3) enlarge the repair budget (multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair trajectories to exercise the repair mechanism. Each recommendation follows from the observed artifact pattern (single shared candidate + universal validator PASS) and is implementable within the same emulation‑grounded framework.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is constrained by the shared_initial_candidate design choice; this is an explicit design factor and not an execution error. Construct validity depends on verifier coverage—deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encodes a finite set of semantic checks and may not cover all subtle operational fault classes. External validity is limited by the synthetic emulation corpus and device images used; extrapolation to heterogeneous production deployments requires further study. Conclusion validity: realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 eliminates statistical power to detect verifier benefit in this configuration; future power planning must account for generator variability and adversary strength to create informative discordant pairs.

Operational implications: Our findings do not imply that deterministic verifiers lack operational value; rather they demonstrate that the choice of generation semantics and adversary exposure in paired designs crucially determines whether a verifier's causal contribution can be measured. Evaluators seeking to quantify verifier benefits should design for opportunities where the generator can produce invalid or risky candidates that the verifier (and repair logic) can meaningfully alter.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: all 240 paired episodes were safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm can only change the paired outcome if the shared candidate fails validation or a repair is applied; in this run shared candidates universally passed validation and no repairs occurred, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We present artifact‑grounded diagnostics and concrete, implementable recommendations (independent generations per arm, stronger/adaptive adversaries, larger repair budgets, improved verifier coverage) to ensure future GVR evaluations can measure verifier causal effect in informative, nondegenerate ways.

disclosure_statement: Execution used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family; the guarded pipeline employed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted at most one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature selection, preregistration, experiment design, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. The archived execution manifest and artifacts (provider‑call and validator traces, task manifests, and analysis outputs) accompany this submission and are the provenance for numerical results reported in the paper.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
